  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bank Teller

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
Minh Nguyen was twenty-four when the coordinated attacks ruptured the city’s transit system. He had been waiting on the platform when the secondary charge detonated near the escalator, sending a concussive wave through the tiled concourse. He had come to believe that the rumble of the underground trains would forever carry the sharp, metallic ring of shrapnel, so when he later heard a sudden clatter at the bank, his shoulders locked before his mind registered the sound of a dropped pen. In the weeks that followed, the memory of the blast did not settle into a neat story; it arrived as fragmented sensations. He would pause mid-sentence, certain that the air itself might still ignite, and his hands would instinctively hover over the counter as if bracing for falling glass. He was certain that if he looked up, he would see the same smoke curling from the ventilation shafts. The daily habits formed quietly but steadily. Minh woke each night at the same hour, alert and still, listening to the refrigerator’s hum and the distant tires on wet asphalt before allowing himself to drift back. He found himself turning in the doorway, scanning the sidewalk behind him to ensure no one was following, a motion that had become as automatic as breathing. When a customer’s voice rose in sudden frustration, Minh’s jaw tightened; he had come to believe that anger was a warning signal, a prelude to something breaking, and he would react with a sharp, disproportionate outburst. His work at the bank became both refuge and trap. He stayed late, processing extra deposits and reconciling accounts, while his hands remained busy and his mind drifted into the quiet where the memory lived. Over the counter, he noticed how easily his certainty in his own judgment had frayed; he second-guessed the amount on a slip of paper, convinced he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him. Divorce had not arrived as a surprise, though Minh understood how his distance had woven into it. He avoided intimacy, and he was certain that closeness required a kind of vulnerability he no longer trusted. He had acted in ways that went against who he was during the attacks; he recalled pushing through a crowd with a clumsiness that felt like betrayal, dropping his wallet, stumbling when he should have stood firm, and later convincing himself that he had failed his own standards. He could not rely on himself to read a room, to judge a threat, to stay composed. When his ex-wife asked why he had withdrawn, he had suppressed the thoughts, pushing the images of the collapsed canopy and the dust-choked announcements into the back of his mind until they quieted. He told himself it was easier to let go, but the truth was that he simply could not carry the weight of another person’s expectations while keeping his own composure intact. By the time he was twenty-six, the accumulated weight had altered the rhythm of his life. The overwork had bled into his personal hours; the avoidance of intimacy had left him sleeping in the guest room, waking alert to the same quiet threats. At the bank, the morning rush became a series of micro-triggers. A sudden door slam made him step back, checking behind him without thinking. He would correct a transaction three times, certain he had misread the figures, and if a customer lingered too long, he would cut the interaction short. The habit of suppression had become his default; he would walk through the city streets with his gaze fixed forward, deliberately not thinking about the trauma, not thinking about the possibility that it might happen again. What frightened him most was not the fear itself, but the certainty that he had lost the ability to trust his own reactions. He sought help because the bank counter, once a place of mastery, now felt like a stage where he might fail publicly, and he hoped to learn how to stay present without bracing for the next blast.
